title: Hazelnut dacquoise disc
subtitle: The nut-meringue base used in layered gateaux and entremet
excerpt: A dacquoise disc is a round of hazelnut meringue baked low and slow until crisp outside and chewy within. It is a building block for layered gateaux: it holds its shape under buttercream or bavarian cream without going soggy, because the fat from the ground hazelnuts waterproofs the meringue slightly.
sourceNotes: Dacquoise is a classic element of French patisserie, used as a structural layer in composed desserts such as the Paris-Brest, the Japonais, and various gateaux. The technique of folding ground nuts into French meringue is documented in Escoffier and in the standard works of modern French patisserie.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked discs between sheets of baking paper in a rigid container. They thaw in 30 minutes at room temperature without losing their texture.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake discs up to 3 days ahead and store in an airtight container at room temperature. They keep well as long as the kitchen is not humid.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 130 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 115 degrees Celsius. Slow bake for 75 minutes, then leave in the turned-off oven for 1 hour.

glossaryTerms.definition: A disc or sheet of meringue folded with ground nuts (hazelnuts, almonds, or a mix). The fat in the nuts partially waterproofs the meringue, giving a chewier, denser result than plain meringue and making it structurally stable under moist fillings. It is a standard layer in French composed gateaux.

content.text: requires dry conditions: any moisture in the bowl, on the whisk, or in the kitchen will prevent the whites from reaching stiff peaks. Toast the hazelnuts first and grind them while still warm; ground nuts that have cooled tend to clump.

items.prepNote: toasted, skins rubbed off, ground to a fine meal in a food processor

content.text: Draw two 20 cm circles on baking paper and place the paper ink-side down on the baking trays. Preheat the oven to 130 degrees Celsius.

Whisk the egg whites with the cream of tartar on medium speed until foamy. Increase speed to high. Add the caster sugar one tablespoon at a time, whisking continuously. When all the sugar is in, whisk until the meringue holds stiff, glossy peaks. This takes 8 to 10 minutes.

Sift the icing sugar over the meringue and add the ground hazelnuts. Fold in with a large spatula in as few strokes as possible to retain volume. Some streaking is acceptable; overfolding deflates the meringue.
Divide the mixture between the two circles and spread evenly to the edge with a palette knife or the back of a spoon. Pipe or spread to an even thickness of about 1.5 cm.
Bake for 75 minutes until the surface is dry and very lightly coloured. Turn off the oven and leave the discs inside with the door slightly ajar for a further 1 hour.
Peel the baking paper carefully. The base of each disc will be firm; the centre will remain slightly chewy. Cool completely before assembling into a gateau.

Spread hazelnuts on a dry baking tray and roast at 180 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes until the skins are cracked and the nuts are light golden. Transfer immediately to a clean kitchen towel and rub vigorously to remove the skins. Not all skins will come off; that is fine. The toasting deepens the flavour significantly.
